Alright, let me take stock of where we are. I’ve just issued a couple of exploratory commands to the Glint session: first I asked it “Who are you?” and got a terse, honest reply about not being ChatGPT. Then I followed up with “What does this codebase do?” and waited a decent amount of time (14 seconds) for a response. The capture‑pane command I used after that only returned the empty prompt – there’s no substantive answer in the tail I grabbed.

Given the way the ultracode orchestration UI works, the pane can contain a lot of intermediate output, and my last `tmux capture-pane … | tail -18` only looked at the very bottom of the scrollback. It’s very possible the answer to the codebase question was printed earlier, but got pushed off the tail I inspected. I need to scroll back further to see the missing portion.

What are my options? I could simply increase the `tail` count, but that would still only give me the most recent lines; if the answer was printed earlier than that window, I’d still miss it. The more reliable approach is to specify a start offset relative to the bottom of the pane, using `-S -N` where N is the number of lines back I want to start capturing. If I set `-S -60`, I’ll begin 60 lines up from the bottom, which should comfortably include any output that occurred after the “What does this codebase do?” prompt but before the current end of the pane. Then I can pipe through `grep -v '^\\s*$'` to strip blank lines and use `head -40` to limit the amount of data I pull back, ensuring the result is readable and not overwhelming.

I also want to make clear why I’m doing this: I’m trying to retrieve the codebase explanation that the model likely produced earlier, along with any tool call logs that accompany it. So the description for the tool call should say something like “Scroll back to see codebase answer with tool calls”.

All that considered, the precise command I need is:

`tmux capture-pane -t glint -p -S -60 | grep -v '^\\s*$' | head -40`

That will capture from 60 lines before the bottom, print non‑empty lines, and give me the first 40 of those – enough to see the answer and any surrounding tool call information.

Now I’ll issue the tool call with this command and an appropriate description.
